learn.hook: Your toothpaste, the steel spoon in your tiffin and even the salt on your chips all contain minerals dug out of the Earth!
points: A mineral is a homogeneous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. Minerals are found in rocks; an ore is an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements, in high enough concentration to be mined profitably.

Types of minerals: metallic — ferrous (iron ore and the minerals used with it to make iron and steel, such as manganese, nickel and cobalt), non-ferrous (copper, lead, tin, bauxite) and precious (gold, silver, platinum); non-metallic (mica, salt, potash, sulphur, granite, limestone, marble, sandstone); and energy minerals (coal, petroleum, natural gas).

Occurrence: in veins and lodes in igneous and metamorphic rocks (tin, copper, zinc, lead); in beds or layers of sedimentary rocks (coal, some iron ore, gypsum, potash salt, sodium salt); from decomposition of surface rocks (bauxite); as placer deposits in the sands of valley floors and hill bases (gold, silver, tin, platinum); and in ocean waters (common salt, magnesium, bromine) with manganese nodules on the ocean floor.
Rat-hole mining, done in narrow tunnels by families in Jowai and Cherapunjee (Meghalaya), has been declared illegal by the National Green Tribunal.
Minerals are finite and non-renewable — they take millions of years to form. We must conserve them by recycling metals, using scrap metal and finding substitutes.

example.q: Gold is sometimes found in the sands of riverbeds far from any gold mine. How?
steps: Gold exists in rocks on hills upstream.
Running water slowly wears away these rocks; gold is not corroded by water.
Heavy gold particles settle in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills — these are placer deposits.
example.answer: Gold settles as placer deposits in river sands after being washed out of rocks upstream.

learn.reallife: Aluminium cans and old steel utensils sent to the kabadiwala are recycled into new metal, saving minerals that took millions of years to form.

revise.summary: A mineral is a homogeneous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure; an ore is a mineral concentrated enough to be mined profitably. Minerals are metallic (ferrous, non-ferrous, precious), non-metallic or energy minerals, and they are finite and must be conserved.

topics.title: Important minerals and where they are found

learn.hook: The Bailadila hills of Chhattisgarh got their name because they look like the hump of an ox — and they are full of high-grade iron ore!
points: Iron ore is the basic mineral and backbone of industrial development. Magnetite is the finest ore (up to 70% iron) with excellent magnetic qualities; hematite is the most important industrial ore by quantity used (50–60% iron).

Iron ore belts: Odisha–Jharkhand (Badampahar in Odisha; Gua and Noamundi in Jharkhand); Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur (Bailadila hills, exported through Visakhapatnam port); Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru in Karnataka (Kudremukh, a 100% export unit, sends ore as slurry by pipeline to a port near Mangaluru); and Maharashtra–Goa (exported through Marmagao port).
Manganese is mainly used in making steel and ferro-manganese alloy — nearly 10 kg of manganese is needed for one tonne of steel. It is also used in bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

Copper (good conductor, used in electric cables): Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand). Bauxite (for aluminium): Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and Bilaspur–Katni plateau; Panchpatmali in Koraput (Odisha). Mica (insulator for electrical and electronic goods): Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt (Jharkhand), Ajmer, Nellore. Limestone is the basic raw material for cement and is used in smelting iron ore.
Mining hazards: dust and harmful fumes cause lung diseases in miners; mines risk roof collapse, flooding and fire; waste and slurry pollute land, soil, streams and rivers.

example.q: Why is mica so useful in the electronics industry?
steps: Mica can be split into very thin sheets.
It has excellent di-electric strength, low power loss and resists high voltage — it insulates well.
So it is used to insulate parts in electrical and electronic equipment.
example.answer: Because mica splits into thin sheets and is an excellent insulator that resists high voltage.

learn.hook: The light in your room may come from coal that began as a swamp forest about 200 million years ago!
points: Conventional sources of energy: firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal). Burning dung cake is being discouraged because it uses up valuable manure.

Coal forms by compression of plant material over millions of years. Grades by rising quality: peat, lignite (low-grade brown coal with high moisture; main reserves at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu), bituminous (most popular for commercial use; metallurgical coal for smelting iron) and anthracite (highest quality hard coal).

Gondwana coal is about 200 million years old and is found mainly in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro). Tertiary coal is about 55 million years old and occurs in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. Coal is bulky, so heavy industries and thermal power stations are located near coalfields.

Petroleum gives fuel for heat and lighting, lubricants and raw materials; refineries are a 'nodal industry' for synthetic textiles, fertilisers and chemicals. Main areas: Mumbai High, Gujarat (Ankleshwar is the most important field) and Assam, the oldest oil-producing state (Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran-Hugrijan).

Natural gas is a clean fuel (CNG for vehicles) and petrochemical raw material, found in the Krishna-Godavari basin, Mumbai High, the Gulf of Khambhat and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The 1,700 km Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) pipeline carries it to western and northern India. Hydel power uses fast-flowing water (renewable); thermal power burns coal, petroleum or natural gas (non-renewable).

example.q: Why are steel plants and thermal power stations usually built on or near coalfields?
steps: Coal is bulky and heavy, so transporting it is costly.
When coal is burnt, it loses weight and turns to ash.
Building the plant near the coalfield saves the cost of carrying large amounts of coal.
example.answer: Because coal is a bulky material that loses weight on burning, so it is cheaper to use it near where it is mined.

learn.hook: The sun, the wind, the tides, the Earth's inner heat and even cow dung can light up India — without running out!
points: Non-conventional sources: solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and nuclear (atomic) energy. They are needed because fossil fuels are limited and cause pollution.

Nuclear energy is obtained by altering the structure of atoms, which releases heat used to make electricity. Uranium and thorium are found in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan; the monazite sands of Kerala are rich in thorium.

Solar energy: India is a tropical country, and photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity. Wind energy: the textbook describes the cluster from Nagercoil to Madurai in Tamil Nadu as India's largest wind farm cluster; Nagercoil and Jaisalmer are well known for using wind energy effectively.

Biogas is made from shrubs, farm waste and animal and human waste; it has higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake and charcoal. 'Gobar gas' plants give two benefits: energy and better-quality manure. Tidal energy: the Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh (Gujarat) and the Sundarbans (West Bengal) have ideal conditions. Geothermal energy: experimental projects at Parvati valley near Manikarn (Himachal Pradesh) and Puga valley (Ladakh).
Conserving energy: 'energy saved is energy produced'. Use public transport, switch off lights and fans when not in use, use power-saving devices and use non-conventional sources.

example.q: A village has many cattle and the families cook with dung cakes. Why would a gobar gas plant be better?
steps: Burning dung cakes is smoky and wastes dung that could be manure.
In a gobar gas plant, dung decomposes to give biogas, a cleaner fuel with higher thermal efficiency.
The slurry left behind is excellent manure for the fields — so the village gets both energy and manure.
example.answer: It gives cleaner, more efficient fuel and also good manure — twin benefits.
